papers.title_in_file: Quantum Federated Learning: Architectural Elements and Future Directions
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section 6 case study results, sections 8 and 9; taxonomy and application sections skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A survey chapter on quantum federated learning with a taxonomy, applications, a fraud-detection case study and open challenges.

assertions.value: The authors report that in a federated fraud-detection case study, derived from the work of Sawaika et al., the QLSTM model outperforms the classical LSTM by approximately 2% in AUC, 5% in Accuracy and 10% in Recall on Dataset 1, and by 3% in AUC, 6% in Accuracy and 4% in Recall on Dataset 2, under a federated setup with five nodes, on 20K data points from each dataset.
quotes: the QLSTM model outperforms the classical LSTM by approximately 2% in AUC, 5% in Accuracy, and 10% in Recall for Dataset 1; and by 3% in AUC, 6% in Accuracy, and 4% in Recall for Dataset 2.
under a federated setup with five nodes.
The results discussed in this study were obtained on 20K data points from both datasets.
assertions.certainty_reason: Case study result the chapter attributes to Sawaika et al. [48]; empirical, from one study, simulated.
assertions.reader_inference: The case study is a prior paper's result summarized in a survey; the figures are read from the text, not re-derived.

assertions.value: The authors report a decreasing performance trend as the number of federated nodes grows in the case study, and attribute it to the smaller dataset available per node for training.
quotes: We observed a decreasing trend with the increasing number of nodes.
This is primarily due to the smaller dataset available per node for training, which limits the local convergence of each model.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical observation from one case study, with the authors' own explanation.

assertions.value: The authors state that most QFL works are at the level of simulation only, that very few papers explored hardware implementations, and that research papers lack a clear justification for using quantum resources.
quotes: Most of the works in the domain of QFL are currently at the level of simulation only.
Very few papers explored the hardware implementations of their proposed QFL frameworks.
the research papers lack a clear justification for using quantum resources
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey authors' characterization of the literature, without a counted basis in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: This bears on any use of QFL results as evidence of hardware performance.

assertions.value: The authors state that, from the surveyed applications, QFL can match or even outperform classical FL models while reducing the time for convergence and enhancing communication safety.
quotes: the QFL can match or even outperform classical FL models while reducing the time for convergence, and enhancing the communication safety.
assertions.certainty_reason: A summary of results the chapter attributes to the surveyed works; no single experiment settles it.
assertions.reader_inference: The same chapter says most works are simulation only, so this is not hardware evidence.

papers.title_in_file: ADIABATIC QUANTUM COMPUTING FOR LOGISTIC TRANSPORT OPTIMIZATION
papers.what_it_is: A thesis-style report on capacitated vehicle routing solved with classical, hybrid and QUBO quantum-annealing methods.

assertions.value: The authors report that the OR-Tools routing algorithm performed better than the QUBO routing equations, with a lower total distance in all the data-sets tested, and that the experiments ran on a classical computer using the Simulated Annealing Sampler.
quotes: the OR-Tools routing algorithm performs better than the QUBO equations, obtaining paths with a lower total distance in all the data-sets tested
the experiments were performed on a classical computed using the Simulated Annealing Sampler
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical comparison from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The routing comparison used a classical simulated annealer, so it is not a test of quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that classical algorithms typically perform better than their quantum counterparts, but that under certain circumstances the quantum clustering algorithm has an advantage over K-Medoids, mainly when the clusterability of the data is lower.
quotes: Classical algorithms typically perform better than their quantum counterparts, though this is not a totally fair comparison
the quantum clustering approach delivers better results.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the conclusion itself notes the comparison is not fair.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 3 states the QUBO equations were solved locally with a simulated annealer and also on D-Wave Advantage; the conclusion does not say which produced the clustering comparison.

assertions.value: The authors state that the largest annealer on Amazon Braket (D-Wave Advantage System 6.1) has a limit of around 145 fully connected variables, and that the embedding complexity decreases the viability of the quantum algorithms for last mile delivery at scale.
quotes: has a limit of around 145 fully connected variables.
the additional complexity of the embedding problem decreases the viability of applying the quantum algorithms for the last mile delivery problem at scale.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' viability judgment plus a hardware figure stated without a source in the passage.

assertions.value: The authors report that the full CVRP QUBO algorithm can only be used on toy problems: for the smallest CMT data-set (CMT01) with 50 customers and 5 vehicles the QUBO has over 10,000,000 variables, and the solver could not find a good solution on a data-set with only 6 customers and 2 vehicles.
quotes: for the smallest CMT data-set (CMT01) with 50 customers and 5 vehicles the resulting QUBO has over 10,000,000 variables
it is unable to find a good solution on a data-set with only 6 customers and 2 vehicles
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

papers.title_in_file: Evidence of Scaling Advantage for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm on a Classically Intractable Problem
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results summary, discussion, methods on quantum minimum-finding
papers.what_it_is: JPMorgan Chase and Quantinuum study of QAOA time-to-solution scaling on the LABS problem, by simulation up to 40 qubits and trapped-ion runs.

assertions.value: The authors report from noiseless exact simulation with up to 40 qubits that the time-to-solution of QAOA with p = 12 layers grows as 1.46N, improved to 1.21N with quantum minimum-finding, against 1.34N for the best classical heuristic.
quotes: We perform noiseless simulations with up to 40 qubits and observe that the runtime of QAOA with fixed parameters scales better than branch-and-bound solvers
We find that the TTS of QAOA with number of layers p = 12 grows as 1.46N , which is improved to 1.21N if combined with quantum minimum-finding.
This scaling is better than that of the best classical heuristic, which has a TTS that grows as 1.34N .
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result from fitted simulations of one problem; not a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The printed exponent is lost in extraction; the figures are the bases of an exponential in N.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not claim QAOA is the best theoretically possible algorithm for the LABS problem.
quotes: However, we do not claim that QAOA is the best theoretically possible algorithm for the LABS problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own claim limit in the Introduction, p.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the main finding is evidence for QAOA as a building block giving speedups on an idealized fault-tolerant quantum computer.
quotes: This provides evidence for the potential of QAOA to act as a building block that provides algorithmic speedups on an idealized fault-tolerant quantum computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own claim in the Discussion, p.7.

assertions.value: The authors report running QAOA on Quantinuum trapped-ion processors for problems with up to N = 18 and state that an algorithm-specific error-detection scheme reduced the impact of noise on solution quality by up to 65%, and that further improvements in error correction and hardware are necessary to implement the minimum-finding variant.
quotes: we implement QAOA on Quantinuum trapped-ion quantum processors (26, 27) on problems with up to N = 18
demonstrate that it can reduce the impact of noise on solution quality by up to 65%.
further improvements in quantum error correction and hardware are necessary to implement the quantum minimum-finding augmented with QAOA.
assertions.certainty_reason: Hardware experiment result from one study.

papers.title_in_file: Classification of the Fashion-MNIST Dataset on a Quantum Computer
papers.what_it_is: Study that improves a variational data-encoding algorithm, encodes Fashion-MNIST, and runs simple variational classifiers on ibmq-kolkata.

assertions.value: The authors report a best test accuracy of about 40% on the quantum computer ibmq-kolkata, computed over only the first 100 test images because of limited access.
quotes: Due to the limited access to ibmq-kolkata, we only compute the test accuracies based on the first 100 images.
Despite the noise present in ibmq-kolkata, we still achieve the best test accuracy of about 40%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical hardware result from one study on 100 images.

assertions.value: The authors display a support vector machine test accuracy of 89.48% as a reference alongside the simulated and hardware classifier accuracies.
quotes: Test accuracy from a support vector machine (see Appendix A) of value 89.48% is displayed for reference
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical figure from one study, given as a reference line.
assertions.reader_inference: Against this reference the 40% hardware accuracy is far lower; the authors present it as a proof of concept.

assertions.value: The authors state that the data encoding circuits and the classifiers are first trained on classical computers and then deployed on the quantum computer, and that they do not focus on searching for a variational classifier with potential quantum advantage.
quotes: The data encoding PQCs and the classifiers are first trained on classical computers and then deployed on the quantum computer.
We do not focus on the search for a variational classifier with potential quantum advantage
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup and scope in the Introduction, p.3, and Discussion, p.7.

assertions.value: The authors report generally lower test accuracies on hardware from circuits with more CNOT gates in total, which they say suggests the benefits of the sparse ansatz.
quotes: We observe generally lower test accuracies from circuits with more CNOT gates in total, suggesting the benefits of the sparse ansatz.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical observation from one study.

papers.title_in_file: Implementing Large Quantum Boltzmann Machines as Generative AI Models for Dataset Balancing
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, sections IV to VII; embedding algorithm details skimmed
papers.what_it_is: Study that embeds a 120 by 120 quantum restricted Boltzmann machine on D-Wave Pegasus to generate synthetic attack samples for the CICIDS2017 intrusion dataset.

assertions.value: The authors report that a QRBM with 120 visible and 120 hidden units was embedded on D-Wave Pegasus and generated 1,683,771 synthetic attack samples, giving a balanced dataset of 4,208,618 samples.
quotes: a QRBM with 120 visible and 120 hidden units was successfully embedded
Repeating this process 1,700 times resulted in 1,683,771 synthetic attack samples, creating a perfectly balanced dataset of 4,208,618 samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one dataset.

assertions.value: The authors state that QRBMs provided superior results to SMOTE and RandomOverSampler, and report under QRBM balancing a Random Forest precision of 96.18% and a Decision Tree precision of 95.94%, while under RandomOverSampler the Decision Tree reached 96.08% precision.
assertions.anchor: Section V and VII, Tables VIII and IX
quotes: Compared to classical techniques such as SMOTE and RandomOverSampler, QRBMs provided superior results while maintaining remarkable computational efficiency.
The Random Forest achieves the highest precision at 96.18%, and the Decision Tree follows closely with a precision of 95.94%.
Decision Tree has a precision of 96.08%, recall of 95.98%, and an F1 score of 95.99%
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical comparison from one study on one dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported tables do not show QRBM ahead of RandomOverSampler for every classifier; the Decision Tree is slightly higher under RandomOverSampler.

assertions.value: The authors report the balancing step took 0.75 seconds for SMOTE, 0.23 seconds for RandomOverSampler and 0.33 seconds for the QRBM.
quotes: The SMOTE and Random Over Sampler methods took a relatively short time (0.75 and 0.23 seconds, respectively), and only 0.33 seconds for the QRBM.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical timing from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The QRBM was not faster than RandomOverSampler in this table, although the abstract speaks of milliseconds.

assertions.value: The authors state that QRBMs have limitations because quantum hardware restricts scalability through limited qubit counts and noise, and that future research should include direct comparisons between QRBMs and GANs.
quotes: However, QRBMs have limitations, as quantum hardware restricts scalability due to limited qubit counts and noise.
Future research should include direct comparisons between QRBMs and GANs
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limits and untested comparison in the Discussion, Section VI.

papers.title_in_file: From Quantum Graph Computing to Quantum Graph Learning: A Survey
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section 5 challenges and outlook; middle sections skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A survey of quantum algorithms for graph tasks, from quantum graph computing to quantum graph learning.

assertions.value: The authors state that the survey focuses on quantum algorithms on graphs, from quantum graph computing to quantum graph learning, which they believe is an emerging field.
quotes: Our survey focuses on quantum algorithms on graphs, from quantum graph computing to quantum graph learning, which we believe is an emerging field.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in the Introduction, p.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that challenges remain due to the restricted scale of current quantum devices, instability of quantum states and the complexity of yielding numerical results by measurement.
quotes: challenges still exist due to the restricted scale of current quantum computational devices, instability of quantum states and complexity of yielding numerical results by measurement.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey authors' statement about the field.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Cerezo et al. 2020, that the cost landscapes of training quantum algorithms are generally non-convex, making it difficult to establish general guarantees about the computational expense of the optimizations.
quotes: The cost landscapes of training quantum algorithms are generally non-convex, making it difficult to establish general guarantees about the computational expense of the optimizations
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Grover 1996, that quantum search has an advantage that is quadratically faster than the most effective classical method for searching and retrieving target values in unstructured databases.
quotes: [Grover, 1996] points to another valuable evidence, showing the quantum advantage of searching and retrieving target values in unstructured databases quadratic faster than the most effective classical method.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work.

papers.title_in_file: Dissipative Quantum Hopfield Network: A numerical analysis
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, sections on trajectories and storage capacity, conclusions
papers.what_it_is: Numerical study of a dissipative quantum Hopfield network of qubits with Lindblad jump operators, simulated with QuTiP.

assertions.value: The authors report that oscillations among stored attractors predicted by a previous mean-field theory emerge only in single trajectory simulations and damp when averaged over many quantum trajectories in finite systems.
quotes: The oscillations among stored attractors reported in a previous meanfield theory for the long-time regime emerge only in single trajectory simulations.
For finite-size systems, oscillations among attractors damp in simulations when one averages over many quantum trajectories.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result from simulations of small systems.

assertions.value: The authors report that for small-size systems the quantum term of the Hamiltonian has a negative effect on storage capacity, while it decreases the probability of being trapped for a long time in mixture or spin-glass states.
quotes: Our study reveals that for small-size systems the quantum term of the Hamiltonian has a negative effect on storage capacity
The inclusion of the quantum term in the system decreases also the probability to be trapped in mixture or spin-glass states for a long time
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result from simulations of small systems.

assertions.value: The authors state that their simulations can only be done for relatively small system sizes, so nothing can be concluded about the mean-field capacity results, and that the steady-state comparison used a very small system size (N = 10).
quotes: only can be done for relatively small system sizes, so one can not conclude anything about these mean-field capacity results.
the very small system size that is used in simulations (N = 10)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own size limit in the storage capacity discussion before Section 4.

papers.title_in_file: State Classification via a Random-Walk-Based Quantum Neural Network
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, main text, results on discrimination and classification, conclusion; supplementary material skimmed
papers.what_it_is: Proposal of a quantum stochastic neural network based on quantum stochastic walks, tested by numerical simulation on state discrimination and entanglement classification.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QSNN approximately reaches the Helstrom bound on the average success probability for binary state discrimination after about 30 iterations, in numerical simulation.
quotes: The average success probability rises rapidly, and after about 30 iterations, it achieves the Helstrom bound.
with numerical simulation. The success probability of the QSNN turned out to be very close to the theoretical optimal success probability, i.e., the Helstrom bound.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that, trained on four samples and evaluated on 49 Werner-like states, the QSNN identifies separable states with probability 0.62 and entangled states with probability 0.75.
quotes: The trained QSNN identifies separable states successfully with the probability of 0.62 and identifies entangled states successfully with the probability of 0.75.
After training with four samples, it can classify a number of states with acceptable accuracy.
while use 49 states with
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QSNN becomes confused about the states at the boundary p = 1/3, though the success probability stays higher than the error probability for each state.
quotes: Although the QSNN becomes confused about the states at the boundary p = 1/3, the success probability is always higher than the error probability for each state.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit on the classification result in the Results section, p.6.
